item.title: “Monks, ‘bait’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Hunter’ is a synonym for Māra. ‘Hunter’s followers’ are a synonym for Māra’s…
item.description:
“Monks, ‘bait’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Hunter’ is a synonym for Māra. ‘Hunter’s followers’ are a synonym for Māra’s followers. ‘Herd of deer’ is a synonym for ascetics and brahmins. Here, monks, the first kind of ascetics and brahmins, entering and indulging, eat the bait cast by Māra and the world’s offerings. Having entered and indulged, they eat those foods, become infatuated; from infatuation, they become heedless; from heedlessness, they become subject to Māra’s will among that bait and those offerings. Thus, monks, these first ascetics and brahmins have not escaped Māra’s power.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 25 – Nivāpasutta

item.title: “And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those forms,…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then that monk, monks, should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ And, monks, there are sounds … odors … tastes … phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then that monk should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ Thus, monks, is non-restraint.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.98

item.title: “A boil, monks, is a synonym for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished with boiled rice and…
item.description:
“A boil, monks, is a synonym for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished with boiled rice and porridge, impermanent, subject to rubbing, pressing, breaking, dissolution, and destruction. It has nine wound openings, nine natural orifices. From these, whatever flows out is inevitably impure, foul-smelling, and disgusting; whatever issues out is inevitably impure, foul-smelling, and disgusting. Therefore, monks, be disenchanted with this body.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.15

item.title: “Monks, for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, this is the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma: dwell often in disenchantment toward…
item.description:
“Monks, for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, this is the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma: dwell often in disenchantment toward form … toward feeling … toward perception … toward formations, dwell often in disenchantment toward consciousness. One who dwells often in disenchantment toward form … toward consciousness fully understands form … feeling … perception … formations … fully understands consciousness. One who fully understands form, fully understands feeling, fully understands perception, fully understands formations, fully understands consciousness, is freed from form, freed from feeling, freed from perception, freed from formations, freed from consciousness, freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.146
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Ānanda, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating…
item.description:
“Ānanda, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having restrained covetousness and sorrow in the world. Ānanda, thus a monk is an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 16 – Mahāparinibbānasutta

item.title: “And how, good sirs, is one not defiled by sensual lust? Here, good sirs, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is…
item.description:
“And how, good sirs, is one not defiled by sensual lust? Here, good sirs, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is not attached to agreeable forms nor repelled by disagreeable forms. He dwells with bodily mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. When he tastes a flavor with the tongue … When he cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he is not attached to agreeable phenomena nor repelled by disagreeable phenomena. He dwells with bodily mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. This, good sirs, is called a monk who is not defiled by sensual lust regarding forms … regarding tastes … regarding phenomena. A monk living thus, good sirs, if Māra approaches him through the eye, Māra does not gain an opportunity, Māra does not gain an object. If Māra approaches him through the tongue … through the mind, Māra does not gain an opportunity, Māra does not gain an object.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.243
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Ānanda, he reflects: ‘Those low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble thoughts that are not connected with the goal and do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace,…
item.description:
“Ānanda, he reflects: ‘Those low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble thoughts that are not connected with the goal and do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna — such as sensual thoughts, ill-will thoughts, harmfulness thoughts — I will not think those thoughts.’ In this way, he is clearly aware of that.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 122 – Mahāsuññatasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: The hair is curled in seven rings, The eyes are rubbed with collyrium and rouge — Enough to fool a fool, But not one who…
item.description:
The hair is curled in seven rings,
The eyes are rubbed with collyrium and rouge —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: “And how, Mahānāma, does a noble disciple guard the sense faculties? Here, Mahānāma, when a noble disciple sees a form with the eye, he does…
item.description:
“And how, Mahānāma, does a noble disciple guard the sense faculties? Here, Mahānāma, when a noble disciple sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise—he restrains that cause, guards the eye, practices restraint of the eye. When the ear hears a sound … nose smells an odor … tongue tastes a flavor … body feels a touch … mind cognizes phenomena, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise—he restrains that cause, guards the mind, practices restraint of the mind. Thus, Mahānāma, a noble disciple guards the sense faculties.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 53 – Sekhasutta

item.title: “Monks, if anyone says: ‘Māra’s complete snare’ — he would speak rightly of women. Indeed, women are ‘Māra’s complete snare.’”
item.description:
“Monks, if anyone says: ‘Māra’s complete snare’ — he would speak rightly of women. Indeed, women are ‘Māra’s complete snare.’”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.55
